analysis.one_liner: Bans banks from making or financing payday loans and voids payday loan contracts.
analysis.headline: The payday loan ban was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in June 2007 and died there without a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any lender to make a payday loan using a borrower's personal check or automatic bank withdrawal, and would bar insured banks from making or financing payday loans directly or indirectly. It would also void payday loan contracts from the start, take effect 30 days after being signed into law, and let borrowers sue lenders for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Cash-strapped borrowers who use payday loans, who would be spared triple-digit-fee loans repaid from their bank account and could recover damages from lenders that violate the ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday loan borrowers with low incomes

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any creditor from making a payday loan backed by a check drawn on, or an automatic debit from, a bank account [S3].

Bars insured depository institutions from making payday loans directly or indirectly, or lending to other lenders to finance payday loans — closing the 'rent-a-bank' route payday lenders used to evade state rate caps [S3].
Declares any payday loan contract covered by the bill void from inception and gives borrowers statutory damages plus all other remedies, including punitive damages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders lose their core product, and banks that made or financed payday loans lose that business. Borrowers who relied on payday loans for emergencies would need to find credit elsewhere, at least in the short run.

drawbacks.text: A total ban rather than a rate cap leaves borrowers who need short-term cash without a substitute, and could push some toward unregulated or offshore lenders [S3].
The ban is tied to loans structured around checks or account debits, so lenders could rework products to fall outside the definition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people stuck rolling over payday loans at effective annual rates that can run several hundred percent, eliminating the product outright is a real gain, and the bill adds teeth by voiding contracts and allowing damages. The honest cost is that it does nothing to create affordable small-dollar alternatives, so borrowers' emergency credit needs remain unmet; the bill bans the harm rather than replacing it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Udall introduced the bill on June 26, 2007 with three Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never left committee and never received a vote in either chamber before the 110th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, which kept making short-term high-fee loans untouched for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders who kept operating untouched

for.name: Tom Udall
for.role: U.S. Representative, New Mexico; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor [S5].

for.name: Luis Gutierrez, Keith Ellison, Jan Schakowsky

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over banking law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote; its only recorded supporters were the Democratic sponsor and three Democratic cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill outlaws their core product and lets borrowers void contracts and sue for damages. Payday lenders profit from fees on short-term loans to cash-strapped borrowers, so their interest runs directly against the borrowers the bill protects.

The bill bars insured banks from making payday loans directly or indirectly and from financing other payday lenders, ending a fee stream some banks earned by lending to payday lenders through 'rent-a-bank' arrangements [S3]. Most large banks' everyday business is unaffected.
